articles.text: An eerie orange haze blanketed Piedmont and the rest of the San Francisco Bay Area on Wednesday, September 9 as an unprecedented outbreak of wildfires continued to burn through California. The smoky conditions caused motorists to use their headlights as early as 8 a.m. and covered buildings, cars and yards in ash. Residents noted that the sun was essentially invisible the entire day. While the striking orange color of the sky disappeared, unhealthy air conditions continued over the next week and are projected to remain in the near term. Some 3.2 million acres have burned in the state so far over the past few weeks, according to CalFire. articles.text: Smoke from raging wildfires across the West Coast continues to cause unhealthy air quality in Piedmont, according to updates from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) on Monday, September 14. The Air District announced that it was again extending its “Spare the Air” alert for the entire San Francisco Bay Area until today, Wednesday, September 16. It is possible the alert could be extended again as well. The extension marks an unprecedented 30 consecutive Spare the Air days, over double the previous record of 14 days of Spare the Air alerts set in 2018. Some 3.2 million acres have burned during this devastating wildfire season so far, Cal Fire said yesterday, Tuesday, September 15. Blazes have also ravaged Oregon and Washington. Smoke from all of these fires have caused terrible air quality in the Bay Area. The severe situation was strikingly evident last Wednesday, September 9, when the skies turned a dark orange color. Although the color dissipated by the following day, the unhealthy air conditions continued. When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those who are sensitive to air conditions. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, September 16, 2020 Opinion How the pool transformed my life By Grace Davies Editor: I am writing to strongly encourage the Piedmont community to vote Yes on Measure UU to provide a much-needed pool to Piedmont. The Piedmont Pool has meant so much to me during the last three years in high school and has helped shape who I am today. When I entered PHS, I was encouraged to try water polo my freshman year. I had never been on a swim team or done much swimming, but thought, why not? That decision changed the trajectory of my whole high school experience. I met the most amazing girls that first year on the water polo team, many older than me who were mentors both in and out of the water. I have cherished my years of water polo and feel the practices, games and team bonding have been some of my best high school memories by far. Being a part of the pool community through water polo opened my eyes to another great skill and opportunity – lifeguarding and teaching swim lessons. The pool provided the training and certifications for me to have a flexible work experience that was also very fulfilling. I can’t imagine a more convenient job for a PHS student. I could walk to work after school and schedule my hours around my other activities. Not only did I earn a paycheck, but I had an impact on others and got to work with a great community of staff at the pool. I’d also like to mention that my grandfather, Bill Drum, was a huge supporter of the Piedmont Pool and an avid lap swimmer. He passed away too soon to see me enjoy “his” pool, but I know he would be out there enthusiastically supporting Measure UU! Please remember the students when you consider your vote -- and how much we all benefit from this project. We need to continue the tradition of a community pool and swimming program in Piedmont. Please vote Yes on Measure UU for the future of swimming in Piedmont. articles.text: Editor: I have known and have worked with Cory Smegal for many years, first as a fellow parent volunteer, and more importantly for the past four years as a School Board colleague. Cory has a deep knowledge of our Piedmont School District honed by years and years of getting involved, rolling up her sleeves, and getting things done. Cory understands that our schools are only as good as the students and staff in them. Cory understands our facilities literally inside and out after spending years on our Facilities Steering Committee. Cory understands the craziness of school funding and our complicated budget. Cory understands how quickly K-12 education is changing right now. Most importantly she understands how it all meshes together. Her knowledge has benefitted all of us, especially now as we have navigate these crazy times. During our regularly scheduled Board meetings and our 14 additional Special Board meetings, Cory has been a calm, reasoned voice, always putting the wellbeing of our staff, community, and most importantly our students front and center. We will be very lucky to have Cory serve our community for the next four years. –Andrea Swenson
articles.title: In support of Cory Smegal for School Board

articles.text: Editor: I have known Hilary Cooper for about 14 years, since our kids were in kindergarten. Now they are sophomores in college. Soon after Hilary moved to Piedmont, we teamed up to co-chair the Spring Fling fundraiser for the three Piedmont elementary schools. We were hesitant because we were both somewhat new to the community. But Hilary led our team with enthusiasm and purpose. She included parents from all three schools and throughout the community. Hilary is extremely organized, and she doesn’t miss a beat, from the smallest details to the most important. The event would not have been possible without her. The following year we co-chaired the Giving Campaign and again, Hilary became the natural leader. Once Hilary commits herself to something, she’s all in. She works behind the scenes to prepare for meetings and events. She is extremely knowledgeable about our community, our schools, and education in general. Her volunteer experience gives her insight into many aspects of the Piedmont schools, from budgets and funding to curriculum and bell schedules. Her past experience as a teacher gives her insight into how things really work in a classroom. Hilary is passionate about education in general, which is why she is willing to commit so much time to making sure our schools are the
articles.title: Hilary Cooper – passionate about education

articles.text: Editor: Conna McCarthy is a gem and Piedmont is very lucky she is running to serve on the City Council. Conna has a family history of community service and involvement which she will carry on with her positive attitude and skills. I personally have worked with Conna in the past on Piedmont High School sports activities and most recently on the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame event, which she successfully chaired. Her great attitude and “can-do” ethic will be a perfect addition to the Piedmont City Council. –Barbee Rubenstein
articles.title: McCarthy lauded for “can-do” ethic

articles.text: Editor: We are fortunate to have had Cory Smegal as a School Board Member for the last four years, and I am even more grateful she is willing to serve another term. Cory is the consummate public servant – conscientious, fiscally responsible, dedicated, and a creative problem solver. Since Board Meetings have been on zoom, I have watched Cory advocate for students first. Her student-centered perspective focuses on their mental health and safety during this unprecedented time. This summer, Cory provided strong board leadership to advocate for in-person instruction until this option was no longer feasible due to state mandates. As an incumbent, Cory knows how to work with administrators, faculty, and families to promote excellence in public education. She has represented Piedmont in Sacramento to advocate for state funding and academic standards. Cory understands the fiduciary responsibilities of the Board and provides strategic leadership to ensure academic excellence. It has been a privilege to work with Cory on Parent Club Boards from Wildwood through Middle and High School. articles.title: Cavenaugh willing to tackle tough issues

Coming together to address the district-wide crises of the day (all of which paled, of course, to 2020), I got to see Hilary in action -- and I became impressed with her ability to connect to different constituencies in our community. As a society – and even as a community – we have become too divisive; we do not value enough those who will listen to people with a different perspective, finding nuance and crafting consensus when the problems feel over-constrained and the combatants have dug in. I believe that Hilary’s ability to understand disparate views and to forge compromise will be a tremendous asset to our school board and to our community. The shadow of the pandemic will be long; we need leaders who are equipped to lead not just through the immediate crisis, but the many challenges to come. articles.text: Theft, vehicle theft, auto & residential burglary significantly up Larceny (theft), vehicle theft and residential burglary incidents increased in 2020 through the second quarter of the year, as compared to the same time period, April-June, in 2019. In a report to Piedmont City Council, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said that total crimes reported jumped from 104 in 2019 to 168 in 2020, which demonstrates a 62 percent increase. Reported burglaries doubled from 17 in 2019 to 34 in 2020. Reports of vehicle thefts also doubled from 11 to 24, and larceny incidents jumped from 67 to 103. Bowers noted that vehicle theft has significantly increased in Oakland this year as well, and a spillover into Piedmont is not surprising. Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) incidents decreased this year, from 165 in 2019 to 121. Reader cameras in Piedmont resulted in the recovery of 15 stolen vehicles and nine arrests. Earlier this year, city council approved expansion of ALPR readers throughout the city; camera readers will be placed at Trestle Glen Road and Park Boulevard, Trestle Glen and Valant Place, Indian Avenue and La Salle, Harvard Avenue and Ranleigh Way, and Blair Avenue and Calvert Court. Vandalism cases were concentrated in the center of town, where most of the schools are located. “Unfortunately the school [district] has had a fair amount of folks going onto school property and damaging property. We are aware of that and are working with the schools to mitigate that the best way we can,” Bowers said. Bowers also noted that there appears to be increased vandalism in parks throughout the city. “One thing we’ve seen is that it appears someone is intentionally vandalizing our parks, by pouring a vinegar solution and killing [grass] in those areas,” he said. Mayor Bob McBain asked Bowers if he had any theories as to why crime, especially theft, has increased this year. “Short of a violent felony, criminals know they can walk away [with little punishment]. It is a factor,” Bowers said. “We need to have a long-term perspective on this, and not jump to too many conclusions [at this point] in the year.”
articles.title: City sees increase in crime in 2020

articles.text: Q: A resident just moved into a mid-20th century home. Two of the bathrooms haven’t been touched since 1953 and the estimated cost to bring them up-to-date is about $37,000. What affordable improvements could be included in a bathroom remodel to meet the proposed requirement? Since the project is more than $25,000, it will need to include at least one energy efficiency improvement. If the home is newly purchased, the home energy score, or home energy audit from the point of sale should be available. To comply with the reach code, the project can include one of the recommendations from those reports. Alternatively, the inclusion of new water efficient plumbing fixtures and the insulation of accessible hot water piping would fulfill the reach code requirements. Q: A resident has already made many low cost energy efficient improvements to their home, including attic insulation, duct sealing, LED lights, and low flow plumbing fixtures. The resident is planning a $78,000 home improvement, not related to the furnace or water heater. Would the resident be required to replace their fairly new gas-burning furnace or water heater? “No, the resident would not be required to replace the new gas-burning furnace or water heater,” stated Szasz. “In this case the resident has already completed all of the ‘low hanging fruit’ efficiency improvements, leaving just heat pumps on the improvement list. However, heat pump installation is beyond the resident’s scope of work.” So in this case, the building official would grant a modification allowing the resident not to install heat pumps. articles.text: The Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present a virtual screening of Suppressed 2020: The Fight to Vote, tomorrow, Thursday, September 17 at 4:30 p.m. The film will be followed by a talk with voting rights advocate Valerie Morishige. Director Robert Greenwald’s urgent and timely film focuses on the Stacy Abrams gubernatorial campaign in Georgia, revealing the rampant voter suppression that affected the outcome of that 2018 midterm election. The film exposes the threat those techniques pose to elections throughout the U.S. in November this year. The 40-minute documentary illustrates the problems of long voting lines and uncounted absentee ballots, and how Brian Kemp, who was both a candidate for governor and the Secretary of State in charge of the Georgia election, put more than 53,000 voter registrations on hold until after the election. Eighty percent of those registrations were filed by Black residents. Not surprisingly, Kemp won the election and is now Governor of Georgia. Voter suppression efforts and failures in the voting process are not limited to Georgia or other “red” states. “We might have all of the fancy policies and politicians saying all the right things about voting in California, but in practice we fail,” said Morishige. “We need to make voting accessible for all,” she said. According to a blockbuster report by the American Civil Liberties Union and just published on September 2, the state of Georgia has been quietly — and illegally — purging hundreds of thousands of valid registered voters from the state rolls for the better half of a decade. Of the more than 300,000 names that were purged from the rolls, the study discovered that “198,351 Georgia voters who supposedly moved from their registration addresses who, in fact, have not moved at all, and therefore were wrongly purged, a 63.3% error rate.” This is a conservative estimate, however, because the report “left out of this list those voters whose addresses we were unable to confirm,” the ACLU explains. Poll workers, who are overwhelmingly seniors and highly vulnerable to the coronavirus, are underpaid and undertrained on the electronic equipment used in some precincts. Many businesses and public facilities can’t or won’t provide space for polling places because of stringent regulations and the added burden of the patchwork of local public health guidelines for COVID-19. These conditions have led to a Voting rights advocate Valerie Morishige will be available for questions following a screening of the film, Suppressed 2020: The Fight to Vote, on Thursday, September 17. scarcity in in-person voting locations, resulting in long lines and missed opportunities to vote. “Pull back that veneer and you see something really rotten happening. It’s almost like termites,” commented Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University, in the film. “We’ve got to understand: this stuff is bureaucratic. It’s mundane. It’s routine. But it is lethal.” Please join the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee for this fascinating, infuriating film and learn how to recognize and prevent voter suppression here in California. For details on how to watch the film and attend the post-film discussion on Zoom, go to the ADFS website at www.diversityfilmseries.org/.
articles.title: Diversity Film Series opens fall with film tomorrow on voting ills

articles.text: On September 3, Piedmont city staff held a virtual town hall meeting to provide an opportunity for residents to learn more about the proposed Reach Codes. A wide variety of concerns were brought up by both councilmembers and residents after the Council’s July 20 first reading of the proposal. A second reading has since been deferred. The panel of speakers included City Planner Kevin Jackson, former Civic Spark Fellow Justin Szasz, and city Plans Examiner Paki Muthig. Q: When did the City choose $25,000 as the trigger point for the Energy Improvement list? Doesn’t that discourage people from getting permits for renovating homes? Would a $50,000 trigger have been better? Staff looked at permit data from the last few years in order to find a threshold that would generate the most progress toward the city’s greenhouse gas emissions goals, while still enabling homeowners to undertake most repairs and upkeep projects. “Seventy-eight percent of total projects [in the city] had a construction cost of under $25,000,” said Muthig. Eleven percent of projects were between $25,000 and $50,000, six percent were between $50,000 and $100,000, and only five percent were over $100,000. “The $25,000 threshold excludes most projects that would be considered necessary repairs, such as roof [repairs] or seismic foundation upgrades,” Muthig explained. Projects above that threshold are the more extensive renovations that can and should easily incorporate measures to increase a home’s energy efficiency, he added.
articles.title: Part 2 in a 2-part series

articles.text: The California State Department of Public Health announced the process for granting TK-5 grade school waivers to eventually allow some in-person learning, even while Alameda County is in the “purple” tier for COVID- 19 restrictions. Speaking at the Piedmont School Board meeting on September 9, Supt. Randy Booker stated that he had submitted an initial survey to begin the process of requesting a waiver for Piedmont’s students in grades TK to 5th for in-person learning. The Intent to Apply form, which gives basic information about the school district’s population, was submitted prior to the September 11 deadline. The actual application to Alameda County’s Public Health Department was originally due on September 17, but that date has been pushed back to October 2. The date adjustment is due in part to a delay in the distribution of the applications to school districts. At press time Piedmont still has not received its application form, and as of September 9, no school district in Alameda County had received the application. The most difficult aspect of the waiver application process Alameda County is still in the purple (most restrictive) tier for COVID- 19 restrictions. PUSD will be required to file a waiver to get elementary school students back to in-person learning. will be to prove that Piedmont School District has a contract with an outside vendor to provide testing to all elementary teachers and staff. Teachers and staff are required to receive testing prior to returning to school, then once every two months. This means a contract needs to be in place for roughly 200 tests. Booker has had a preliminary discussion with Kaiser Permanente. The application will require districts to outline plans for cleaning, disinfecting, ventilating, face coverings, health screenings and hygiene practices. Much of these plans are already outlined in Piedmont School District’s Memorandum of Understanding with staff and teachers. Even after applications are submitted, the Alameda County Public Health Department has advised that waiver requests will not be approved or denied for at least five weeks. The earliest Piedmont’s elementary schools could reopen through the waiver process would be in November. However, if Alameda County were to move out of the purple zone to red (less restrictive), the waiver would not be necessary. “If we move to red and stay there for two weeks, we would then be permitted to bring back all students,” said Booker.
articles.title: PUSD begins waiver process for grade school classrooms

articles.text: Piedmont High School student Hamza Mahmood displays two freshly baked loaves of sourdough bread. Just a few months ago, I was in my biology class learning about fermentation and the role it plays in making sourdough. We had to turn in a loaf of bread at the end of the project. Mine was passable for the class, but as a loaf it was as hard as a rock and flat as a frisbee. Making sourdough is really a lot harder than it seems, I discovered. If someone had told me then that soon the entire world would grind to a halt, I would have called them crazy. But lo and behold, the impossible came to pass. We were all locked in our houses like pets in their kennels, only allowed to leave for necessities of life. The pandemic has been hard on everyone, but for some, it has been much worse. As businesses everywhere shut down, hardearned jobs halted. All of a sudden many people were left with no income. As a family who is more fortunate, we felt that it was our duty to help those in need. Through my grandparents’ nonprofit organization, we bought masses of food and ran several food pantries and delivered groceries to people in need. I didn’t help all that much during these food pantries; I had to stay in the car because of COVID. But I was inspired and wanted to do more. But what and how? First, I needed to pick a charity for my donations, and I wanted to pick an organization that spoke to me. I decided on the American Red Cross because I liked how it is an impartial organization providing help to people regardless of their skin color, religious beliefs, race, class or political opinions. I also like how they provide care where it’s needed most, regardless of the danger they have to face. In addition, I felt more of a connection with the Red Cross and the work that they do because it is my ambition to become a physician. But I needed to figure out how to raise money for the Red Cross. I sat and brainstormed. What was a simple way to raise money? An idea came to me. Something that we were all taught in elementary school. A bake sale. But what would I sell? My sourdough of course. If I could get good at baking sourdough and have a fundraiser for charity, I had the potential to raise a lot of money. So, the idea was set, but the bread wasn’t. I needed practice. I baked loaf after loaf, each better than the last. Slowly but surely, I was improving, and finally, I was ready to give my bread away. We started with the neighbor, and as our bread production increased, so did our demand. All sorts of people asked for loaves as we got better at baking them. As we gave bread to people, the donations started to rack up. $100, $200, $1000, all the way to $2000. We had more than doubled our goal of $1000. With all of these donations, I felt good about the community service. It was a wonderful feeling to give someone a loaf and see their eyes light up as they thank you for something you put so much time, energy and love into. Every time we gave away a loaf of bread, I felt like I was contributing to something bigger than myself. I felt like I was giving somebody a gift that they really enjoyed and were thankful for. Winston Churchill once said, “We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give.” He was absolutely right. Hamza Mahmood is a sophomore at Piedmont High School.
articles.title: Hamza Mahmood – a student donating loaves to charity

articles.text: The Associated Student Body at Piedmont High extended its annual Club Day from one day to two days last week, and though everything was virtual using Google Meet, the result was a bonanza for the school. A total of 39 student organizations and clubs signed up at lunchtime on Thursday and Friday, most likely a record high. With school entrenched in distance learning, the clubs at PHS look to fill a large void in extracurricular activities and involvement between students. Connections between students outside of class have suffered, so the role of Club Day took on added meaning this year. “Club Day was more exciting this year, because it really allowed people to find something to do besides school. I have seen a lot of new clubs that people are really passionate about,” explained ASB president Grace Davies. This initial involvement with clubs is particularly impressive especially because not all existing clubs have started up, as they are not required to participate in Club Day. For example, the popular Kiva Club, which fundraises to give micro loans to people, has not begun yet. A new club, Teens4Biden, started by ASB senior class president Audrey Edel, had the highest enrollment on Club Day. At their first meeting last week, club members signed up to volunteer in various capacities. “There were more activism clubs, and some new, really creative clubs this year,” noted Edel. “There was a larger variety overall, which shows that some of our peers are dedicated and trying to uplift each other and make a difference in the school community.” Not every club had a big turnout, but of the students that did attend, there seemed to participate and engage more than in previous years. “I think it forced people to more of a commitment. You have to listen (on Zoom) to what the club presidents are saying; you can’t just put your name down and leave,” Edel said. Clubs can be created, and students can join clubs at any time throughout the year. There’s a club for everyone at PHS, including the Diversity Club, Piedmont for Consent, the Astronomy Club, the High Adventure Club and the Asian Student Union. experience College Prep first-hand.

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, September 16, 2020 SchOOLs PUSD begins waiver process for grade school classrooms By Jay Russell The California State Department of Public Health announced the process for granting TK-5 grade school waivers to eventually allow some in-person learning, even while Alameda County is in the “purple” tier for COVID- 19 restrictions. Speaking at the Piedmont School Board meeting on September 9, Supt. Randy Booker stated that he had submitted an initial survey to begin the process of requesting a waiver for Piedmont’s students in grades TK to 5th for in-person learning. The Intent to Apply form, which gives basic information about the school district’s population, was submitted prior to the September 11 deadline. The actual application to Alameda County’s Public Health Department was originally due on September 17, but that date has been pushed back to October 2. The date adjustment is due in part to a delay in the distribution of the applications to school districts. At press time Piedmont still has not received its application form, and as of September 9, no school district in Alameda County had received the application. The most difficult aspect of the waiver application process Alameda County is still in the purple (most restrictive) tier for COVID- 19 restrictions. PUSD will be required to file a waiver to get elementary school students back to in-person learning. will be to prove that Piedmont School District has a contract with an outside vendor to provide testing to all elementary teachers and staff. Teachers and staff are required to receive testing prior to returning to school, then once every two months. This means a contract needs to be in place for roughly 200 tests. Booker has had a preliminary discussion with Kaiser Permanente. The application will require districts to outline plans for cleaning, disinfecting, ventilating, face coverings, health screenings and hygiene practices. Much of these plans are already outlined in Piedmont School District’s Memorandum of Understanding with staff and teachers. Even after applications are submitted, the Alameda County Public Health Department has advised that waiver requests will not be approved or denied for at least five weeks. The earliest Piedmont’s elementary schools could reopen through the waiver process would be in November. However, if Alameda County were to move out of the purple zone to red (less restrictive), the waiver would not be necessary. “If we move to red and stay there for two weeks, we would then be permitted to bring back all students,” said Booker. By Hamza Mahmood Just a few months ago, I was in my biology class learning about fermentation and the role it plays in making sourdough. We had to turn in a loaf of bread at the end of the project. Mine was passable for the class, but as a loaf it was as hard as a rock and flat as a frisbee. Making sourdough is really a lot harder than it seems, I discovered. If someone had told me then that soon the entire world would grind to a halt, I would have called them crazy. But lo and behold, the impossible came to pass. We were all locked in our houses like pets in their kennels, only allowed to leave for necessities of life. The pandemic has been hard on everyone, but for some, it has been much worse. As businesses everywhere shut down, hardearned jobs halted. All of a sudden many people were left with no income. As a family who is more fortunate, we felt that it was our duty to help those in need. Through my grandparents’ nonprofit organization, we bought masses of food and ran several food pantries and delivered groceries to people in need. I didn’t help all that much during these food pantries; I had to stay in the car because of COVID. But I was inspired and wanted to do more. But what and how? First, I needed to pick a charity for my donations, and I wanted to pick an organization that spoke to me. I decided on the American Red Cross because I liked how it is an impartial organization providing help to people regardless of their skin color, religious beliefs, race, class or political opinions. I also like how they provide care where it’s needed most, regardless of the danger they have to face. In addition, I felt more of a connection with the Red Cross and the work that they do because it is my ambition to become a physician. But I needed to figure out how to raise money for the Red Cross. I sat and brainstormed. What was a simple way to raise money? An idea came to me. Something that we were all taught in elementary school. A bake sale. But what would I sell? My sourdough of course. If I could get good at baking sourdough and have a fundraiser for charity, I had the potential to raise a lot of money. So, the idea was set, but the bread wasn’t. I needed practice. I baked loaf after loaf, each better than the last. Slowly but surely, I was improving, and finally, I was ready to give my bread away. We started with the neighbor, and as our bread production increased, so did our demand. All sorts of people asked for loaves as we got better at baking them. As we gave bread to people, the donations started to rack up. $100, $200, $1000, all the way to $2000. We had more than doubled our goal of $1000. With all of these donations, I felt good about the community service. It was a wonderful feeling to give someone a loaf and see their eyes light up as they thank you for something you put so much time, energy and love into. Every time we gave away a loaf of bread, I felt like I was contributing to something bigger than myself. I felt like I was giving somebody a gift that they really enjoyed and were thankful for. Winston Churchill once said, “We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give.” He was absolutely right. Hamza Mahmood is a sophomore at Piedmont High School.

articles.text: How does it translate online? Often, the classroom culture is what makes kids want to go to school and enjoy being there. Key words associated with a strong classroom culture include safe, pleasant, interesting, social, and community. Fostering a classroom culture that embodies these elements can be challenging in a virtual format. Humor plays a key role in creating a strong, positive learning environment. Nuanced communication skills, such as humor, are easily lost in socially distant learning spaces. One of the most common forms of humor naturally occurring in an in-person educational environment is the spontaneous, harmless violation of expectations. That is, something is funny if it contradicts one’s sense of how things are supposed to be. The shared experience of this surprising (and benign) contradiction creates community and increases morale (recall the power of “private jokes”). Shared humor increases feelings of social support, and is relationship building. Humor can also enhance the actual learning process. Shared laughter is a powerful way to reinforce learning. Humor can both capture and maintain students’ attention. For example, in an initial assessment I may include some humor with the immediate purpose of establishing rapport. More often than not, months or even years later, that child will remind me of the humor we shared in that first office visit. Lastly, and perhaps most important at this time, shared humor dampens conflict and enhances feelings of safety. Humor can be an effective coping mechanism to lessen or buffer psychological distress. Surely this is something we want to generalize to online learning. Elements that make humor effective include pacing, timing, economy of expression, vivid language, and the ability to read and respond to the energy of the group. Without the richness of verbal and non-verbal communication of in-person situations, the opportunities for shared humor decreases, and the margin for miscommunication and misunderstanding increases virtually. For example, consider the role that timing plays with humor. Digital platforms can make it difficult to know when to talk, why there may be a pause, and can be generally disruptive to the natural back and forth between students and teachers. Periods of silence create a natural conversational rhythm in real life discussions. However, when on a video call those pauses become unnatural and stressful. With regard to being able to read and respond to the energy of the group, virtual platforms make this increasingly challenging as well. It can be tricky to read key elements of discourse and humor such as body language, eye contact and facial expressions given a digital platform. By maintaining constant visual gaze at the screen, rather than shifting our gaze back and forth between people and actions as would be typical in person, we focus on too few visual cues instead of the full range of body language that we would normally be gathering. essary to demonstrate artificial eye contact on video), teachers and students both may miss other important visual cues. Since the spontaneous opportunities for humor, amusement and delight will likely be diminished with distance learning, parents and teachers can rely on more intentional and deliberate opportunities. For example, we can ask students to build humor into occasional writing assignments. We can add a humorous item to a test, or assignment. Humorous quotes or cartoons can be circulated, and maybe Fridays can be “Joke day.” Language-based humor, based more heavily on multiple meanings, allusion, puns and plays on words, can help to mitigate the loss of spontaneous, situational humor of the in-person classroom. Katie Pengilly, MA,CCC,SLP, is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

articles.text: Simplified Mandarin will be taught online through Zoom technology in small classes this fall through Piedmont Language School. The school offers Mandarin and Spanish before and after school. It is a non-profit designed to help students ages 5-12 enjoy learning Mandarin and develop a strong foundation in learning Chinese language and culture. • Early Mandarin Early Mandarin is for the youngest students (TK to 1st grade) and provides a foundation for learning at the higher levels. The class is taught in themes primarily using simple crafts, rhymes, storytelling and games. The class meets on Mondays from 9:00– 9:40 a.m., and Wednesdays from 2:45–3:25 p.m. • Conversational Mandarin Conversational Mandarin includes Lower and Upper Levels. It is designed to further develop and practice conversational Chinese skills. Classes will be small to ensure an opportunity for each student. Each week will have a theme to guide conversations. The class meets on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 2:45– 3:25 p.m. • Advanced Mandarin Advanced Mandarin is for students entering middle school who have studied previously and are eager for more. The class meets on Mondays at 3:05 p.m. and Wednesdays at 3:25 p.m. The Fall Session for all classes is September 15 to November 19. Winter and Spring sessions will also be available for the yearround program. For more information contact Blair Page, PLS Executive Director, at 652-5229 or by e-mail at: piedmontlanguageschool@ gmail.com. Registration is now open at: https://www.homeroom. com/sites/piedmont-language-school-piedmont.
articles.title: Mandarin classes start this week at Piedmont Language School

articles.text: Does your teenager want to explore their creative voice? The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is offering a new online vocal music course for high school students. Future Voices: Foundations of Vocal Music guides young people through a semester of training in vocal technique, rhythm and harmony, music literacy, and a special virtual choir project. The skills you will learn will support you in choir, musical theater, solo vocal lessons, and songwriting. No prior musical experience is required. The course will meet weekly on Tuesdays from 6:30 - 8:00 pm on Zoom, beginning on Tuesday, September 8. The semester runs from September 8, 2020 through January 9, 2021. PEBCC instructor Tim Silva is a skilled vocalist, singer-songwriter, and musicianship coach with a special gift for sparking creativity in young people. Please contact instructor Timothy Silva (tsilva@piedmontchoirs.org) and the registrar, Anastasia Fegbeitel-Finn (afegbeitel-finn@piedmontchoirs.org), to enroll. Based upon student interest, an AP Music Theory course may also be offered. Contact PEBCC Artistic Director Eric Tuan (etuan@piedmontchoirs.org) if interested in this offering.
articles.title: Advanced vocal music course offered by Piedmont Choirs for high school students

Lake Chabot Boat Rental Boating and Fishing Here’s a new adventure: Take your kids boating at Lake Chabot. Its boat rental service is a well-kept secret. Take a visit for a fun day on the water in any sort of vessel. Try your hand at boating while getting great exercise on row boats, kayaks (single and double), or pedal boats. Prefer a more leisurely time on the water? Electric motorboats are also available in four different sizes: a four-person boat, 16-foot boat with a Bimini top, electric pontoon patio boats, or a tour boat for 20 people. There’s even a bait shop on the dock for kids who want to learn to fish. Bay Area Discovery Museum Outdoor Museum – Now Open Located in Sausalito, in the shadow of the Golden Gate Bridge at Fort Baker, the Bay Area Discovery Museum is worth the trip. Throughout the outdoor museum’s 7-1/2 acres, children up to age 10 will be enthralled with the exhibits, landscapes, activities and installations. There’s a gravel pit, a crow’s nest, a fishing boat and a shipwreck for kids to play on. While there you can also enjoy the beautiful scenery with expansive trails for walking and hiking in the natural beauty of this unique locale. Find recipes and videos on the site, where 9- and 11-year old kids are the only chefs. Choose the skill level of your child and let them work their way up. In no time your kid will have a leg up on a lifelong necessary skill. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew, a coed Venturing unit under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council, holds an annual garage sale. Money raised is used to fund major projects, including building a Tiny House to provide housing for a homeless teen in Oakland, feeding the elderly, and renovating the home of an elderly low- income Oakland resident. Due to COVID-19 and the limitations imposed by Alameda County’s Shelter-in-Place order, the annual fundraiser will be ONLINE this year. To make this a success, we need the support of everyone in the community. We will be soliciting items from residents and selling the donated items online. If you have items you would like to donate, please email us at pcscgaragesale@gmail.com and include a description of the item with a photo. If you are interested in purchasing an item, please visit the “Garage Sale 2020” section https://www.pcservicecrew.org/garagesale on the crew website (pcservicecrew.org). Additional items will be added weekly so please check back with us.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Service Crew Garage Sale Fundraiser Goes Online

Take a visit for a fun day on the water in any sort of vessel. Try your hand at boating while getting great exercise on row boats, kayaks (single and double), or pedal boats. Prefer a more leisurely time on the water? Electric motorboats are also available in four different sizes: a four-person boat, 16-foot boat with a Bimini top, electric pontoon patio boats, or a tour boat for 20 people. There’s even a bait shop on the dock for kids who want to learn to fish. Bay Area Discovery Museum Outdoor Museum – Now Open Located in Sausalito, in the shadow of the Golden Gate Bridge at Fort Baker, the Bay Area Discovery Museum is worth the trip. Throughout the outdoor museum’s 7-1/2 acres, children up to age 10 will be enthralled with the exhibits, landscapes, activities and installations. There’s a gravel pit, a crow’s nest, a fishing boat and a shipwreck for kids to play on. While there you can also enjoy the beautiful scenery with expansive trails for walking and hiking in the natural beauty of this unique locale. Spatulatta Kids cooking website Spatulatta is a fun website that will help kids learn how to become master chefs, or at least not go hungry when on their own. Find recipes and videos on the site, where 9- and 11-year old kids are the only chefs. The writing style of Spatulatta was designed for latch-key kids, and the recipes go to great lengths to make sure a child working alone could figure out what to do. Choose the skill level of your child and let them work their way up. In no time your kid will have a leg up on a lifelong necessary skill. Learn how to make a Tuscan bean dip, an end-of-the-summer salad, and Yumbo Gumbo. More Info: Lake Chabot Boat Rental 17936 Lake Chabot Rd. Castro Valley, (510) 247-2526 www.lakechabotrecreation.com Piedmont Community Service Crew Garage Sale Fundraiser Goes Online The Piedmont Community Service Crew, a coed Venturing unit under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council, holds an annual garage sale. Money raised is used to fund major projects, including building a Tiny House to provide housing for a homeless teen in Oakland, feeding the elderly, and renovating the home of an elderly low- income Oakland resident. Due to COVID-19 and the limitations imposed by Alameda County’s Shelter-in-Place order, the annual fundraiser will be ONLINE this year. To make this a success, we need the support of everyone in the community. We will be soliciting items from residents and selling the donated items online. If you have items you would like to donate, please email us at pcscgaragesale@gmail.com and include a description of the item with a photo. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: hear their perspectives and support their efforts including PUSD School Board, Piedmont Connect, League of Women Voters, Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, Parent Clubs, Piedmont Community Service Crew, Appreciating Diversity Film Series, Piedmont Parent Network, Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign, and others. 2 – Measure UU is a very important ballot measure for Piedmonters. It’s about whether we want to continue to have a local pool facility for Piedmonters to learn to swim, for exercise, relaxation, injury rehabilitation, youth employment, school PE programs including adaptive PE, and HS sports teams. Or Not. It’s that simple. I’m volunteering with the campaign to reach voters so they know our 56-year-old pool is broken and is due to be permanently closed. The City has run out of cost-effective repairs, and it makes no fiscal sense to spend even more money on a failing pool that no longer meets the needs of our residents. Measure UU provides an opportunity for us to come together as a community and design a safe, affordable, and sustainable pool facility for our children and grandchildren to enjoy for the next 50 years. I am optimistic that voters understand what is at stake, and will vote Yes on Measure UU to rebuild the pool. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – I will have several ways residents can reach me: • Phone calls: I will have set office hours and be available for phone calls. Residents can also leave voicemails without requiring a call back. • Email: Residents can email me at their convenience and I will answer within 24 hours. • Zoom Chats: My website will continue to offer individual or group chat sessions with easy online scheduling. • Town Hall Forum: A Zoom event where I give my Council report and City issues can be discussed in a public forum. These events can happen as issues arise or on a scheduled basis. • Monthly Newsletter: After the Town Hall, I will post the event highlights to my website and email a newsletter to subscribers. There will be links in both to contact me. Post-Covid, I would love to meet in person with any Piedmont group or resident during my office hours. 2 – I am cautiously optimistic. The Community Pool For Piedmont group is doing a great job communicating with residents. They have a good website, informative flyer and a hard-working phone banking team. Everyone I’ve talked with is supporting the measure. Those who were undecided have changed to a “yes” vote after we talked it through. This is a difficult time to ask residents to pay more property tax. I understand and am sensitive to that. Non-users of the pool are initially reluctant to support the measure. However, after discussing, most agree the return on investing about 75 cents/day (median Piedmont home) for a new pool is a good one. We don’t want to be the only school district in Alameda County without access to a pool. Our schools are why people move here and why our property values stay high. I remain hopeful that we will vote “yes” on Measure UU. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – An upside to sheltering-in-place is that almost everyone is now expert in scheduling and participating in zoom conversations. Throughout my campaign, I have engaged residents via zoom. I became adept using Facetime and What’s App when one son was in Peace Corps in Ukraine and another son served with the US Navy in Yokosuka, Japan. I am easily contacted through my personal email and cell phone. If modern technology proves problematic, I have a home office and live near the center of town. Constituents are welcome to visit me post-pandemic. I do not foresee any barriers to making myself available to residents. I welcome and want to hear all thoughts, concerns, ideas and questions. 2 – Although passing Measure UU presents unique challenges, I remain very optimistic. While City Council candidates must achieve a plurality, passage of Measure UU requires a supermajority of almost 67%. Dozens of committed volunteers are spending their weekends walking door-to-door addressing voters’ concerns and convincing two-thirds of those voters that Piedmont’s 56 y/o pool has unfixable problems, is unsafe for public use and, most importantly, if Measure UU fails, the pool will permanently close. Piedmonters want a community pool. A survey taken months before Measure UU was placed on the ballot revealed 61% of Piedmonters consider our pool a valued community asset. As more voters understand that our pool must be replaced or permanently closed, we will reach two-thirds approval. ‘Yes on Measure UU’ signs are on display throughout Piedmont evidencing widespread community support. Review the facts at www. communitypoolforpiedmont.com We can’t let Piedmont become the only public school district in Alameda County without access to a local pool. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

I also share them with city staff so they are informed of residents’ concerns and can follow up as necessary. articles.text: original building in that it will be accessible and will include offices, expanded lobby space and classrooms for drama and set design. An initial effort to build a new theater fell through, but a subsequent measure that included building a new science and technology facility was approved. The new Alan Harvey Theater was originally scheduled to open at the start of the 2021 school year; however, pandemic related construction delays may mean a later completion date. HILARY COOPER 1 – I am deeply committed to serving our students and am happy to make myself available to Piedmont residents for questions or comments. I believe that listening is a critical component of serving on the school board. As Parent Club President at PMS & PHS, I worked with teachers, parents and administrators and made myself available to all of them. I also hosted many parent and administrator coffees, and I have always valued opportunities for our community to come together. If elected, I hope to continue to be a resource for all of our community members. I will have a designated email, and if some prefer to speak to me directly, I am happy to chat in person or over the phone. I look forward to working with our community and I will always be just a phone call or email away. 2 – Our school district is in the midst of two new building construction projects, a new STEAM building and the new Alan Harvey Theater, both at PHS. Both projects are funded by the $66M improvement bond (Measure H1). Over the past few years, I have had the opportunity to substitute teach at PHS and I have seen the need firsthand for infrastructure improvements. I was thrilled when Measure H1 passed and I am excited to see the new STEAM building, and in a year or so, the new Alan Harvey Theater. Alan Harvey Theater was one of our district’s most heavily used venues -- from speaker series to assemblies to musicals, it was packed multiple times a week. Once completed, I believe the new Alan Harvey Theater will be a source of great pride for our community. JASON KELLEY 1 – In addition to being available by email and phone, I would make a point of reaching out to school and community groups, to attend group meetings, and to solicit feedback and input from residents. As a parent who is in almost daily contact with teachers and other parents at all three school levels, I am already aware of many of the day-to-day concerns about our school district. It’s important for Piedmont residents to be able to easily communicate with their elected representatives and to know that their concerns are being heard and addressed. Being accountable to the voters is especially key in a small community such as ours. 2 – Alan Harvey was one of my teachers in high school and I performed in school musicals under his direction at the old theater, so I’m very excited about the new building. Arts education is so important to help students learn confidence and creative thinking. I’m proud that Piedmont has a strong tradition of supporting arts education and want to ensure that continues and grows. As a producer for four years of the biggest performing arts event in Piedmont, Beach Revue, I got to see first-hand how children learn from performing on stage. They become more comfortable speaking in front of groups and more confident in their own abilities. The new Alan Harvey Theater will allow more Piedmont students to gain those skills before heading to college or work, and it will be a great training facility for students who want to pursue careers in the performing arts. HARI TITAN 1 – I would make sure my email and cell number are published in the student directory and available to the local press and school district. The most convenient form of communication these days is email, however, emails sent to influence public officials are part of the public decision-making record and subject to disclosure. For confidential matters, it is better to make an appointment and discuss those matters over the phone. For school district policy matters, I would like to start moderated online wiki pages that would allow residents to quickly get up to speed on anything the board or district is working on and also make it easier to contribute to the decision-making process at a time that is convenient to each resident. This Web 2.0 facility should also reduce the volume of multiple emails to the board with the exact same advice. 2 – I have many articles on my harititan.com/search/node/aht website presenting financial arguments for a new Alan Harvey Theater. In 2014 the school board presented a plan to renovate and add classroom space to the old Alan Harvey theater. Through articles in the Piedmont Post, I discovered that our renovation cost estimate was comparable to what other school districts were paying for a brand new theater. The benefits of designing a brand new theater included 2-stories with more stadium-style seating, much better acoustics, handicap access, net-zero energy, and earthquake safety. I also analyzed our 2014 cost estimate for a brand new theater and discovered it was nearly double what other districts paid. Since labor and material costs were independent of Piedmont as a job site, I promoted getting competitive guaranteed maximum price bids for a new theater. In 2016, the district obtained much lower bids and added a new Alan Harvey Theater to Measure H1. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – Over the past four years as a School Board member, I’ve tried to make myself very accessible to all constituents. As Board correspondent for two years, I responded to all emails received on behalf of the Board. I also responded to all emails that I personally received. Pre-pandemic, I met with people in person. I’ve also reached out to people that have spoken at our Board meetings to get clarification on their views. I’ve talked to people on the phone and I’ve gone on walks with people. I am very happy when people provide input to the Board. I really try to listen to all viewpoints because I think that is the best way that decisions get made. 2 – I am very familiar with the new Alan Harvey Theater. For the last two years, I’ve served as Board liaison to the Facilities Steering Committee. This committee reviews all aspects of the current construction program and makes recommendations to the Board. Construction began in earnest on the new Performing Arts Center with the Alan Harvey Theater this spring once the schools had closed to students. It will be completed in the Fall of 2021 and includes a 487-seat auditorium, (459 fixed, 28 movable seats; the original AHT had 442 seats), a green room with dressing rooms, a separate drama classroom to minimize wear and tear on the main stage, a drama department office and a conference room. If you would like to see some renderings of the new theater, please go to: https://measureh1.org/background/updates/09-2018-update. html#new-harvey-theater-update. Once the new Performing Arts Center is completed, it will be an amazing school and community resource. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

It’s about whether we want to continue to have a local pool facility for Piedmonters to learn to swim, for exercise, relaxation, injury rehabilitation, youth employment, school PE programs including adaptive PE, and HS sports teams. Or Not. It’s that simple. I’m volunteering with the campaign to reach voters so they know our 56-year-old pool is broken and is due to be permanently closed. The City has run out of cost-effective repairs, and it makes no fiscal sense to spend even more money on a failing pool that no longer meets the needs of our residents. Measure UU provides an opportunity for us to come together as a community and design a safe, affordable, and sustainable pool facility for our children and grandchildren to enjoy for the next 50 years. I am optimistic that voters understand what is at stake, and will vote Yes on Measure UU to rebuild the pool. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – I will have several ways residents can reach me: • Phone calls: I will have set office hours and be available for phone calls. Residents can also leave voicemails without requiring a call back. • Email: Residents can email me at their convenience and I will answer within 24 hours. • Zoom Chats: My website will continue to offer individual or group chat sessions with easy online scheduling. • Town Hall Forum: A Zoom event where I give my Council report and City issues can be discussed in a public forum. These events can happen as issues arise or on a scheduled basis. • Monthly Newsletter: After the Town Hall, I will post the event highlights to my website and email a newsletter to subscribers. There will be links in both to contact me. Post-Covid, I would love to meet in person with any Piedmont group or resident during my office hours. 2 – I am cautiously optimistic. The Community Pool For Piedmont group is doing a great job communicating with residents. They have a good website, informative flyer and a hard-working phone banking team. Everyone I’ve talked with is supporting the measure. Those who were undecided have changed to a “yes” vote after we talked it through. This is a difficult time to ask residents to pay more property tax. I understand and am sensitive to that. Non-users of the pool are initially reluctant to support the measure. However, after discussing, most agree the return on investing about 75 cents/day (median Piedmont home) for a new pool is a good one. We don’t want to be the only school district in Alameda County without access to a pool. Our schools are why people move here and why our property values stay high. I remain hopeful that we will vote “yes” on Measure UU. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – An upside to sheltering-in-place is that almost everyone is now expert in scheduling and participating in zoom conversations. Throughout my campaign, I have engaged residents via zoom. I became adept using Facetime and What’s App when one son was in Peace Corps in Ukraine and another son served with the US Navy in Yokosuka, Japan. I am easily contacted through my personal email and cell phone. If modern technology proves problematic, I have a home office and live near the center of town. Constituents are welcome to visit me post-pandemic. I do not foresee any barriers to making myself available to residents. I welcome and want to hear all thoughts, concerns, ideas and questions. 2 – Although passing Measure UU presents unique challenges, I remain very optimistic. While City Council candidates must achieve a plurality, passage of Measure UU requires a supermajority of almost 67%. Dozens of committed volunteers are spending their weekends walking door-to-door addressing voters’ concerns and convincing two-thirds of those voters that Piedmont’s 56 y/o pool has unfixable problems, is unsafe for public use and, most importantly, if Measure UU fails, the pool will permanently close. Piedmonters want a community pool. A survey taken months before Measure UU was placed on the ballot revealed 61% of Piedmonters consider our pool a valued community asset. As more voters understand that our pool must be replaced or permanently closed, we will reach two-thirds approval. ‘Yes on Measure UU’ signs are on display throughout Piedmont evidencing widespread community support. Review the facts at www. communitypoolforpiedmont.com We can’t let Piedmont become the only public school district in Alameda County without access to a local pool. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received. By Allyson Aleksey Part 5 in a series In advance of the municipal election on November 3, School Board candidates were asked two questions: 1) If elected, how would you make yourself available for questions or comments from Piedmont residents. 2) How familiar are you with plans for the new Alan Harvey Theatre? The Post will ask each candidate two questions every week. Responses are listed below. VERONICA ANDERSON THIGPEN 1 – As a School Board member, I would be available to constituents who have questions or who are seeking information about school policy. I would also seek opportunities to include community and youth perspectives in decision-making. I experienced the efficacy of this approach when I engaged with community advocates from the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) joining with teachers, youth and district administrators to craft racial and educational equity policies that have gained widespread support. I see this as a template for board practice. 2 – The new Alan Harvey Theatre will be the result of a yearslong campaign to revamp the aging PHS/MHS campus. It is one of two new facilities that will be built for the $66 million project, which also includes updating five existing buildings and remodeling the outdoor amphitheater. The design for the new Alan Harvey Theater addresses shortcomings of the School Board Election – Candidates Q&A original building in that it will be accessible and will include offices, expanded lobby space and classrooms for drama and set design. An initial effort to build a new theater fell through, but a subsequent measure that included building a new science and technology facility was approved. The new Alan Harvey Theater was originally scheduled to open at the start of the 2021 school year; however, pandemic related construction delays may mean a later completion date. HILARY COOPER 1 – I am deeply committed to serving our students and am happy to make myself available to Piedmont residents for questions or comments. I believe that listening is a critical component of serving on the school board. As Parent Club President at PMS & PHS, I worked with teachers, parents and administrators and made myself available to all of them. I also hosted many parent and administrator coffees, and I have always valued opportunities for our community to come together. If elected, I hope to continue to be a resource for all of our community members. I will have a designated email, and if some prefer to speak to me directly, I am happy to chat in person or over the phone. I look forward to working with our community and I will always be just a phone call or email away. 2 – Our school district is in the midst of two new building construction projects, a new STEAM building and the new Alan Harvey Theater, both at PHS. Both projects are funded by the $66M improvement bond (Measure H1). Over the past few years, I have had the opportunity to substitute teach at PHS and I have seen the need firsthand for infrastructure improvements. I was thrilled when Measure H1 passed and I am excited to see the new STEAM building, and in a year or so, the new Alan Harvey Theater. Alan Harvey Theater was one of our district’s most heavily used venues -- from speaker series to assemblies to musicals, it was packed multiple times a week. Once completed, I believe the new Alan Harvey Theater will be a source of great pride for our community. JASON KELLEY 1 – In addition to being available by email and phone, I would make a point of reaching out to school and community groups, to attend group meetings, and to solicit feedback and input from residents. As a parent who is in almost daily contact with teachers and other parents at all three school levels, I am already aware of many of the day-to-day concerns about our school district. It’s important for Piedmont residents to be able to easily communicate with their elected representatives and to know that their concerns are being heard and addressed. Being accountable to the voters is especially key in a small community such as ours. 2 – Alan Harvey was one of my teachers in high school and I performed in school musicals under his direction at the old theater, so I’m very excited about the new building. Arts education is so important to help students learn confidence and creative thinking. I’m proud that Piedmont has a strong tradition of supporting arts education and want to ensure that continues and grows. As a producer for four years of the biggest performing arts event in Piedmont, Beach Revue, I got to see first-hand how children learn from performing on stage. They become more comfortable speaking in front of groups and more confident in their own abilities. The new Alan Harvey Theater will allow more Piedmont students to gain those skills before heading to college or work, and it will be a great training facility for students who want to pursue careers in the performing arts. HARI TITAN 1 – I would make sure my email and cell number are published in the student directory and available to the local press and school district. The most convenient form of communication these days is email, however, emails sent to influence public officials are part of the public decision-making record and subject to disclosure. For confidential matters, it is better to make an appointment and discuss those matters over the phone. For school district policy matters, I would like to start moderated online wiki pages that would allow residents to quickly get up to speed on anything the board or district is working on and also make it easier to contribute to the decision-making process at a time that is convenient to each resident. This Web 2.0 facility should also reduce the volume of multiple emails to the board with the exact same advice. 2 – I have many articles on my harititan.com/search/node/aht website presenting financial arguments for a new Alan Harvey Theater. In 2014 the school board presented a plan to renovate and add classroom space to the old Alan Harvey theater. Through articles in the Piedmont Post, I discovered that our renovation cost estimate was comparable to what other school districts were paying for a brand new theater. The benefits of designing a brand new theater included 2-stories with more stadium-style seating, much better acoustics, handicap access, net-zero energy, and earthquake safety. I also analyzed our 2014 cost estimate for a brand new theater and discovered it was nearly double what other districts paid. Since labor and material costs were independent of Piedmont as a job site, I promoted getting competitive guaranteed maximum price bids for a new theater. In 2016, the district obtained much lower bids and added a new Alan Harvey Theater to Measure H1. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – Over the past four years as a School Board member, I’ve tried to make myself very accessible to all constituents. As Board correspondent for two years, I responded to all emails received on behalf of the Board. I also responded to all emails that I personally received. Pre-pandemic, I met with people in person. I’ve also reached out to people that have spoken at our Board meetings to get clarification on their views. I’ve talked to people on the phone and I’ve gone on walks with people. I am very happy when people provide input to the Board. I really try to listen to all viewpoints because I think that is the best way that decisions get made. 2 – I am very familiar with the new Alan Harvey Theater. For the last two years, I’ve served as Board liaison to the Facilities Steering Committee. This committee reviews all aspects of the current construction program and makes recommendations to the Board. Construction began in earnest on the new Performing Arts Center with the Alan Harvey Theater this spring once the schools had closed to students. It will be completed in the Fall of 2021 and includes a 487-seat auditorium, (459 fixed, 28 movable seats; the original AHT had 442 seats), a green room with dressing rooms, a separate drama classroom to minimize wear and tear on the main stage, a drama department office and a conference room. If you would like to see some renderings of the new theater, please go to: https://measureh1.org/background/updates/09-2018-update. html#new-harvey-theater-update. Once the new Performing Arts Center is completed, it will be an amazing school and community resource. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of the Argus Leader Piedmont High 2016 graduate Gabe Watson has transferred to the University of Texas after leading Division 2 football in rushing with Sioux Falls in 2018. Piedmont High has a running back on his way to pursuing a potensial career in the National Football League. Gabe Watson, Piedmont High 2016 graduated and the Piedmont Post’s two-time Athlete of the Year (2015-2016), has signed with the University of Texas as a graduate transfer student for the 2020 season. The Big-12 and the Longhorns got their season started last Saturday, September 12 with a 59-3 thrashing of University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP). Still adjusting to the offense, Watson did not appear. “I feel about as good as I can,” Watson told the Argus Leader. “I’m bigger, faster and stronger. My hamstring is fine and getting stronger. To be honest, the quarantine grind has been treating me well. I feel fantastic. Watson led the nation in rushing yards among Division 2 schools in 2018 with 177.9 yards per game, set a school rushing record with 1,957 yards. He had 11 games of over 100-yards that season. He was a finalist for the Harlon Hill Trophy in 2018, considered the Heisman Trophy for Division 2 schools. But the following season he suffered a hamstring injury in the opening game and missed the rest of the year. “Last year was a really tough situation,” Watson said. “I was super tight with that senior class and it was tough to watch from the sidelines.” Watson now joins a crowded backfield alongside Keaontay Ingram, Roschon Johnson and freshman Bijan Robinson. Notably, Ingram and Johnson were the school’s top-two runners from 2019, meaning Watson will work his way up from the bottom. Despite battling for carries in a talented group, the Longhorns are well aware of the importance of having a plethora of options in their backfield. Last year, UT suffered multiple injuries at the position and eventually had to use a quarterback and defensive players as replacements. Known for his frame, speed, and inside running ability, Watson certainly has the characteristics of a first-down, short-yardage, and goa-line running back. Now a Gabe Watson was the Piedmont Posts Athlete of the Year in 2015 and 2016. Longhorn, Watson enters a pipeline to the NFL even if he doesn’t get significant playing time as a fifth-year senior. A member of a major football program within the Big-12 Conference, Watson will be eligible to attend the Pro Day workouts next offseason if he chooses to, and the following local prospect workout days for the Dallas Cowboys and Houston Texans, even the San Francisco 49ers, given that he is a California resident. For those unaware, college Pro Days differ from the NFL Combine in that the annual combine invites around 335 players to the Indianapolis headquarters. Pro Days, on the other hand, brings coaches and scouts to meet prospects on campus for those who didn’t participate in the combine, or those looking to stand on their numbers. It is essentially a job fair for prospects, offering a more exclusive experience and is an arguably more important time for draft eligible players than the combine itself. It leads to private workouts and interviews with staff members, enabling incumbent rookies to make an impression on teams. Watson, a former straight-A student at Piedmont High, certainly has the skills and acumen to make it all the way.

articles.text: Linda Beach Playfield reopened to the public on Monday this week, September 14. Linda Beach Playfield was reopened this week on Monday, September 14, after about seven weeks of closure. The city closed the playfield on July 24 due to lack of compliance by users with the Alameda County Public Health Department’s shelter-in-place orders. Despite repeated warnings from city staff, visitors continued to play group sports, and social distancing was not observed. The field was the first public open space to be closed due to non-compliance of County Health guidelines during the coronavirus pandemic. The closure was followed one week later by the school district closing Witter Field, the largest sports field in the city. The city is asking residents and park visitors to wear a face covering, practice social distancing, and not share sports equipment with members outside of your immediate household. The use of shared sports equipment by groups outside of your household, or “social bubble”, is still not allowed by the county. Only the entrance on Linda Avenue near the Oakland Avenue Bridge will be opened for park access. During public use hours, a park ambassador will be at the entrance and will remind users of and enforce COVID-19 safety requirements. The playfield will be open Monday through Friday, 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. On Saturdays it will be open from 3 p.m. to dusk, and from 9 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. Sunday mornings. Linda Beach Playfield will also be used by the Recreation Department and youth sports organizations by permit only. No public use is allowed outside of the slotted times above. For more information contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at 510-420-3070 (prd@ piedmont.ca.gov).

Piedmont tiptoed home with a 17-14 win. But that was last year, and this year is unlike any other. With the season delayed until December, current PHS football coach Jerome Johnson is visiting his family in Los Angeles. It will be th first time he has been without football in the fall. He’s patiently waiting to hit Phase 3 of COVID protocols, much like the rest of his team – and all other hgh school teams in California. “I’ve just accepted the reality and I’ve set my clock to December,” Johnson said recently. “I’m still in offseason mode. I’ve had to acknowledge that this is beyond my control and we can only adjust to the circumstances.” Plugging along with a virtual offseason program, Johnson has reprogrammed and prepared for the path ahead. “I’m pretty patient. articles.text: Piedmont’s cross-country team in 2005. At this time last year, the cross-country teams under Jeanine Holmlund were just getting their season underway at the Lowell Invitational, where Sophia Zalewski was getting her historic senior campaign underway. The last time we looked back at the cross-country program, we mentioned the North Coast Section championship boys’ and girls’ teams of 2003. We made reference to the 2005 boys’ team as the last team to win both the NCS and State championship. Here, we take a look at the 2005 Division 4 State Champs, and the 2006 NCS runners-up. In 2005, the entire 2003 championship team returned as upperclassmen. At the State Championship at Woodward Park, Mark Ceraldi, then a junior, led the talented team with a fifth-place finish in 16:04 against 195 other runners. Senior Ricky Griffith placed seventh in 16:11. Piedmont had all five of its runners in the top-40: Jesse Baldridge, a junior, finished in 29th in 16:51, senior Dylan McCalmont placed 42nd in 17:00, and Nahoa Moya-Smith was 46th in 17:02. They defeated 2nd place Big Bear to win the State Div. 4 championship by 24 points.
