pages.text: Wednesday, September 16, 2020 25 Obituary Linda Trowbridge died on August 28 Linda Patrice Trowbridge, a Piedmont resident for 37 years, passed away on August 28, 2020 after battling cancer for six years. She was 65. First and foremost, Linda was a wonderful partner and spouse, a loving mother and an elated and doting grandmother. She raised three wonderful children, all left mourning her with their spouses, Brian (Diana), Daniel (Kaitlin) and Patrice (Matt). Linda was overjoyed by the arrival of her now 2 year old granddaughter, Cecilia (Ceci), who “misses grandma already.” In addition to her children and grandchild, Linda is survived by Jeff. her husband of 42 years, and her beloved Cocker Spaniel, Emerson. You would think a stage 4 ovarian cancer diagnosis in 2014 might slow down and define a person. But not Linda, who kicked its butt for almost six years, resolving work issues and planning family engagements up to her next to last day. Born in Casper, Wyoming on September 27, 1955, she met Jeff, her husband to be, at Golden High School in Colorado at age 15. Marrying after obtaining BA degrees at the University of Colorado, Linda and Jeff headed to the Bay Area, where she obtained her MBA at San Francisco State Linda Trowbridge passes away on August 28 after a six-year battle with cancer. well as being a board member of Hospice East Bay. Linda loved working with youth, and served in various positions with her sons’ Boy Scout troop in Piedmont. She was Troop Committee Chair, sending Troop 15 Piedmont Scouts off to many amazing High Sierra backpacking trips and community service activities. After her sons obtained their Eagle Scout awards, Linda offered her executive talents, skills and empathy to approximately 70 young men in Piedmont to shepherd them through the process of obtaining their Eagle Scout awards. Linda was recognized by the Piedmont Council for such service in 2018 with the Sidney C. Singer Service to Youth Award. Linda met with and counseled many of such young men while actively undergoing cancer treatments. Linda co-led a Girl Scout troop in Piedmont, with members of such troop, including her daughter, obtaining the Gold Award. Linda insisted that the Girl Scouts have all of the advantages and challenges of the Boy Scouts, including working on and satisfying Boy Scout merit badge requirements and camping. Linda loved her church, College Avenue Presbyterian Church, serving on its Board of Elders. Linda and Jeff enjoyed cheering on the Oakland A’s baseball team. Linda helped pave the way for future ovarian cancer patients, participating in aggressive studies and treatments and entering into a clinical trial at Mayo Clinic requiring significant travel to Rochester, Minnesota, during the last several months of her life. Linda was a tireless, loving, loyal, champion of her family, friends, co-workers and those in need. Linda was an amazing listener, always genuinely interested in learning more about her family, friends, and colleagues. She loved traditions, family gatherings, and events, and had the ability to make a celebration out of any activity or gathering. The family thanks Linda’s long-time caring providers, Gary Cecchi, MD, and Robin Fernandez, NP. Linda’s beloved charities include: CEI (cei.elders.org), Hospice East Bay (hospiceeastbay.org), Piedmont Boy Scouts (piedmontbsa. org) and College Avenue Presbyterian Church (capcoakland.org). Donations in Linda’s name to any of these organizations would go to amazing good works. A celebration of life for Linda will be scheduled in the future as COVID-19 permits. and began a 35-year career as a healthcare executive. She worked for the Sisters of Providence Health System, Catholic Healthcare West (now Dignity Health), St. Joseph Health System and Kaiser Permanente. where she was the Executive Director for the Continuum for Northern California. While serving on the Board of Directors of On Lok Lifeways in San Francisco, Linda became a great advocate of PACE programs (Program of All-inclusive Care for the Elderly). PACE programs are dedicated to providing frail, mostly low income elders with an alternative to nursing home care. When an opportunity opened up to lead such an organization, Linda jumped at the chance. During the last seven years of her life, including six years while managing her own cancer, Linda served as the CEO of the Center for Elders Independence in Oakland. In that role she greatly increased the number of elders served, opened up and staffed new beautiful day centers, and advocated strongly with state and federal regulators for the program she loved. articles.text: Editor: Piedmont needs Jen Cavenaugh’s re-election to the City Council. Jen brings her energy, enthusiasm and business acumen to keeping Piedmont a wonderful place to live. She provides thoughtful analysis, based on careful inquiry into underlying facts and options, to the Council’s decision-making. Having known Jen for years, she is focused relentlessly on the need to improve the City’s deteriorating infrastructure, an issue long ignored, while remaining fiscally prudent. She also has emphasized the City’s need for strategic planning across its operations, and participation in the effort to respond to climate change. We need motivated and talented people who are willing to serve their community. Please join me in voting to re-elect Jen. –Richard Raushenbush
articles.title: Cavenaugh brings energy, knowledge to the job

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to encourage Piedmonters to re-elect City Council member Jen Cavenaugh. Jen is a Whirling Dervish of energy and dedication to Piedmont. She always does her homework and is very aware of the fiscal issues facing our wonderful City. Jen will continue to work hard to find the best solutions. As an incumbent, she has the experience, common sense and knowledge to “hit the ground running” when the new Council is sworn in. A busy mom of three teenagers, Jen still manages to fit in occasional trips down the coast to surf with her kids. Please vote to re-elect Jen Cavenaugh. Piedmont needs her energy and continued commitment to making Piedmont the best it can be. –Patty White Former Mayor
articles.title: Jen Cavenaugh – helping Piedmont be the best it can

articles.text: Regarding Measure UU, I would like to address the sports of swimming and water polo and the City’s need for a local, viable, competition pool. When living in Oakland, my husband and I joined Orinda Park Pool; we wanted our three daughters to learn how to swim. What was then an innocent priority became the tail that wagged the dog. All three loved swimming for Park Pool Swim Team and every summer was spent transporting them through the tunnel to swim practice and meets. We moved to Piedmont and the girls looked forward to participating on the high school swim and water polo teams. We were surprised by what we found. The situation at the community pool was untenable. The school was at odds with the pool membership. Lane space was at a premium. The swim team was driving to other cities to practice. Water polo team was trying to practice while community pool members tried to swim laps. The pool wasn’t even deep enough for regulation play. The parents met to discuss how difficult it was for the school to reserve swim and water polo times. Talk circulated. How could the pool be redesigned to accommodate necessary changes? . .This was in the 1990s! It is time for the Piedmont community to support the building of a community pool complex. The reasons are irrefutable. Swimming is an essential life skill. Everyone must learn to swim. Safety demands it. Swimming supports all levels of ability and ages. It’s an inexpensive, lifetime, low impact sport. Children improve and gain confidence as they learn different strokes. Seniors improve endurance, muscle strength and cardiovascular fitness. With a proper pool, Piedmont could support a community swim team and a masters swim program. Piedmont High School needs a serviceable, city pool, both for swimming and water polo. Let’s support a swim tradition in Piedmont by voting YES on Measure UU. Everyone benefits.
articles.title: Everyone will benefit with a new pool

articles.text: Editor: I am honored to enthusiastically support Cory Smegal for a second term on the Piedmont School Board. I am grateful for Cory’s unending dedication to our schools over the past 16 years, and especially over the past four years on the School Board. I am continually impressed with her thoughtful feedback during School Board meetings and her ability to work collaboratively with parents, teachers, students, District staff, other School Board members as well as with other districts. Cory’s clear communication and willingness to stand up for what she believes is best for our children and teachers is exactly what we need – especially during these uncertain times. articles.text: Editor: I believe that, for a variety of reasons, many Black, Latino, Asian and other minorities have faced financial roadblocks in finding economic success. It is indisputable that pre-Pandemic, President Trump’s policies ushered in the best economy our country has seen in decades. This resulted in enhanced minority opportunities judged by the following: 1) Lowest minority unemployment rates, including minority youth, seen in decades; 2) Highest minority home ownership, 3) Opportunity Zones, enabling minority entrepreneurs: 4) Funding Black Colleges; 5) Stock Market Highs, helping increase 401 Ks; 6) Signed historic criminal justice reform; 7) Lifted 2.4 million out of poverty; among other policies such as lowering taxes, and bringing back jobs from overseas. President Trump did this with the most vitriolic hatred aimed at anyone I’ve ever seen. In spite of this, he is on his way to rebuilding the economy to its former heights. This coming election is a choice between socialism and free enterprise. Socialism never worked anywhere. If you want to help minorities, vote for President Trump. It certainly worked before and will again. –Mary Lou Weggenmann
articles.title: A vote for Trump

articles.text: I am writing to share my strong support for Measure UU. Let me preface this by saying that I don’t like getting wet. I hate being cold. And, to this day I believe there is a great white shark waiting for me at the bottom of every body of water. The reason I support a new and improved community pool is because swimming saved my life. Five years ago at the age of 47, I injured my lower back (bulging discs L4 and L5). I was in crippling pain. The doctors prescribed drugs, rest, and ice. Months passed and my situation did not improve. MRIs, steroids and cortisone shots did nothing for the pain. I was getting depressed. After months of agony, a good friend begged me to try swimming. Keep in mind at this point I was not a swimmer, but I was desperate for exercise and was willing to try anything to get my life back. My first swim lesson did not go well. I spent the hour holding on to the side of the pool learning how to blow bubbles. In a few weeks of swimming, my back was significantly better.

articles.text: The number of total COVID- 19 cases in Alameda County is now 20,022 as of Monday, September 14, making it the first and only county in the San Francisco Bay Area to surpass the threshold of 20,000 cases. The number of new cases added per day has been relatively low in the county over the past seven days, with 31 cases added as of Sunday, September 13. This is a marked decrease since the peak of 425 daily new cases recorded on August 13, a record high according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. Tragically, 32 more deaths have been recorded over the past seven days in Alameda County, increasing the total number of fatalities to 332. Last Friday, September 11 was the deadliest day yet of the coronavirus pandemic in the Bay Area, with 34 deaths recorded across the region. The majority occurred in Alameda and Santa Clara counties. No new cases of COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, were recorded amongst Piedmont residents. The total number of cases for the City stands at 33, with only one new case reported so far in September. In Oakland, the most populous city in the county, the number of cases since the pandemic was declared in March is now 7,959. In Hayward, 2,857 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,354 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,091. The rolling seven-day percentage of positive tests has trended slightly downward through September, with 5 percent of COVID-19 tests now coming back positive in Alameda County. Santa Clara County, the initial epicenter of the pandemic until cases shot up in Alameda County in June, has recorded a total of 19,613. Contra Costa County has a caseload of 15,489. San Francisco has recorded a total of 10,430 and San Mateo County has recorded 9,242. Along with 29 other counties in California, Alameda County remains in the state’s Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier for reopening businesses and other activities as per a new system put in place by the state government on August 31. Alameda County started the new system in this most restrictive tier after being put on a state “watchlist” back on July 12. There are four color-coded tiers in the new system that have different rules for how the economy can be reopened. San Francisco, Santa Cruz, Santa Clara and Marin counties are all currently in the slightly less restrictive red tier. On Friday, September 11, the Alameda County Public Health Department updated its health orders to allow for vehicle-based gatherings for live music, religious services and other events. Officials also worried about a possible spike from the Labor Day holiday. Because symptoms of the virus can take some time to develop and so many carriers can be asymptomatic, it will likely be several days before officials will know whether the holiday weekend resulted in an increase in cases. Statewide, the total number of COVID-19 cases recorded so far is now 760,013 and there have been 14,451 deaths. California has by far the most cases of COVID-19 in the United States and is the only state with over 700,000 cases. The City of Piedmont keeps its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www. piedmont.ca.gov/government/ covid-19

Do they have to install an electric heat pump furnace? “No, not at all,” Jackson said. “Most furnace replacements are less than $10,000. If renovations amount to less than $25,000, it would be exempt from the reach code requirements.” Q: A resident is developing the basement and crawlspace area into a family room with a half bath. The total project cost will be greater than $100,000, and the resident will be relocating the furnace and water heater as part of the project. Does the resident have to replace their gas furnace and water heater with electric heat pumps? No, according to Jackson. The ordinance does not require anyone to replace their gas furnace with a heat pump, or a gas water heater with a heat pump. However, projects that total more than $100,000 must include two energy-efficient improvements. Q: Are there any rebates available to Piedmonters to help pay for a heat pump? Including all available rebates, about how much would it cost a resident to install a heat pump compared with a new gas furnace and water heater? Rebates available to Piedmont residents currently are through Bay Area Regional Energy Network; they offer a $1000 rebate to replace a gas heating system with a heat pump, explained Muthig. PG&E is only offering rebates for ‘smart thermostats.’ “Due to the wide range of homes in Piedmont, it is difficult to give an exact cost, but it generally is in the $15,000-$20,000 range.” Q: The federal government has minimum efficiency standards for gas furnaces. Can the ordinance set more stringent efficiency standards for new gas furnaces installed in Piedmont? No, it cannot. State and local governments are prohibited from adopting higher minimum efficiencies than the federal standards, confirmed Jackson. Q: Will a resident need to install solar panels when they: get a $25,000 renovation, replace the roof material of their home, or install a new underlayment under roof tiles? No, a resident will not need to install solar panels in any of these cases, according to Muthig. Residents will only need to install solar panels if they are adding an entire new upper level to their house, or increasing their total roof area by 30 percent or more. Q: A resident is planning to increase their home’s floor and roof area by 50 percent. Will they need to install solar panels? Yes, if a resident is increasing their total roof area by 30 percent or more, they need to install solar panels. Q: If a house is undergoing a significant expansion and is required to install solar panels, how will the city determine the number or solar panels that must be installed? The California Energy Code already requires that newly constructed homes have rooftop solar panels, and the energy code has a formula for determining the number of solar panels that must be installed based on the floor area, Szasz said. Piedmont’s Reach Code uses the same formula, making it consistent with the California energy code formula. Q: What if a house is increasing roof area by 40 percent, but the roof is shaded so solar panels are impractical, would the house still be required to install solar panels? In this case, it would not. “The California Energy Code also has a list of exceptional cases in which a new home would not need to install solar panels,” Szasz said. The list of exceptions form the California Energy Code would also be applied. Q: Why does the ordinance require the installation of solar panels on existing houses getting a new upper level, or increasing roof area by 30 percent or more? “The goal is to move Piedmont and the electrical grid to local renewable sources of energy. The state of California is requiring that by the year 2045, all electricity in use in California be generated by renewable sources,” Jackson said. To meet this goal, and Piedmont’s climate action goals, the plan includes requiring the installation of solar panels. Q: A resident is renovating the landscaping of their backyard, installing an outdoor kitchen and reconfiguring the swimming pool to add a spa. The project is expected to cost $175,000. Would the proposed Ordinance affect this project in any way? No. Projects that do not alter the buildings structure are not subject to the ordinance. The resident might explore options to include electric appliances in an outdoor kitchen to reduce their carbon footprint, but it is not required, according to Jackson. The City Council has not yet set a date for the second reading of Reach Codes. articles.text: It has been 19 years and one week since the Twin Towers fell in a terrorist attack in New York City and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001. Ripples of the attacks were felt coast to coast, and no one was spared from the destruction that day. In Piedmont, a giant American flag was raised in solidarity and residents held an impromptu candlelight vigil at the Exedra in the middle of town. Nineteen years ago, a nation came together, united by tragedy.

articles.text: For Betsy Lim, three weeks in Morocco during Ramadan was fascinating and full of wonderful experiences mingling with local families and educators. Three days glamping in the Moroccan Sa­ hara desert allowed her to reconnect with the zillions of stars that she rarely sees in the cities. Even with the constant discoveries in the medinas, souks and in the Sahara desert, she magically found time to catch up with news from home.
